Justification:
### Radial Shaft Seal Analysis & Selection (SKF HMSA10 V)

In-wheel drivetrain design, the radial shaft seal forms the sealing barrier between the rotating wheel hub and the stationary upright.

It fulfills two non-negotiable operational requirements:
1. **Internal Fluid Retention:** Sealing the internal oil without leakage under dynamic track accelerations.
2. **External Contaminant Exclusion:** Preventing dust, track derived particles and other liquids from contaminating the gearbox oil consequently damaging the internal components.

This document provides a comparative engineering trade-off analysis explaining why the **SKF HMSA10 V** was selected over all alternative architectures (HMS5, RG/NBR, CRW1, CRWA1, Cassette seals, and PTFE seals).

---

#### 2. SKF Nomenclature
The designated part is standardized according to **ISO 6194-1** and **DIN 3760**:

$$\mathbf{85 \times 100 \times 9 \quad HMSA10 \quad V}$$

| Code Element | Engineering Definition |
| :---: | :--- |
| **85** | Shaft Diameter ($d_1 = 85\text{ mm}$) |
| **100** | Housing Bore Diameter ($D = 100\text{ mm}$) |
| **9** | Seal Width ($b = 9\text{ mm}$) |
| **HMS** | Rubber Outside Diameter |
| **A** | Auxiliary Dust Lip |
| **10** | SKF Generation 10 Geometry |
| **V** | Fluoroelastomer (FKM / Viton®) |

---

#### 3. Comparative Decision

1. **Outer Diameter Construction:**
   * **Metal Cased (CRW1 / CRWA1): REJECTED.** Aluminum bore expands $88\ \mu\text{m}$ more than the steel case at $100^\circ\text{C}$, causing loss of press-fit so oil leakage.
   * **Rubber Covered (HMS5 / HMSA10): PASSED.** Elastic beaded rubber maintains continuous static contact pressure across all thermal cycles.

2. **External Contamination Exclusion:**
   * **Single Lip (HMS5): REJECTED.** No dust lip, outside contaminants can enter.
   * **Dual Lip (HMSA10): PASSED.** Secondary lip acts as a seal barrier against outside contaminants.

3. **Elastomer Compound:**
   * **Nitrile NBR (Suffix RG): REJECTED.** Dynamic contact temperature reaches $95\text{--}105^\circ\text{C}$ and RG seals are rated to a maximum of $100^\circ\text{C}$.
   * **Fluoroelastomer FKM (Suffix V): SELECTED (SKF HMSA10 V).** Continuous $200^\circ\text{C}$ rating.

---

#### 4. Rationale

##### 4.1 Rubber Outside Diameter (HMS) vs. Metal Outer Case (CRW1 / CRWA1)
The wheel hub and upright are CNC-machined from aerospace-grade **Al 7075-T6**. Aluminum has an exceptionally high coefficient of thermal expansion compared to the low-carbon structural steel (DC04 / AISI 1008):
* $\alpha_{\text{Al 7075-T6}} = 23.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$ *(Source: ASM Handbook Vol. 2 & MMPDS-01)*
* $\alpha_{\text{Steel (DC04)}} = 11.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$ *(Source: Shigley Table A-5 & DIN EN 10130)*

During track runs operating temperatures can reach $T_{\text{op}} \approx 100^\circ\text{C}$ ($\Delta T = 80\text{ K}$ above a $20^\circ\text{C}$ shop assembly).

For the housing bore diameter $D = 100.0\text{ mm}$:

$$\Delta D_{\text{Al}} = D \cdot \alpha_{\text{Al}} \cdot \Delta T = 100.0 \cdot (23.4 \times 10^{-6}) \cdot 80.0 = \mathbf{0.1872\text{ mm}} \quad (187.2\ \mu\text{m})$$

$$\Delta D_{\text{Steel}} = D \cdot \alpha_{\text{Steel}} \cdot \Delta T = 100.0 \cdot (11.7 \times 10^{-6}) \cdot 80.0 = \mathbf{0.0936\text{ mm}} \quad (93.6\ \mu\text{m})$$

$$\Delta \text{Clearance Expansion} = \Delta D_{\text{Al}} - \Delta D_{\text{Steel}} = 0.1872 - 0.0936 = \mathbf{0.0936\text{ mm}} \quad (\mathbf{93.6\ \mu\text{m}})$$

**The Failure Mechanism of Metal-Cased Seals:** An unconstrained thermal expansion differential of $93.6\ \mu\text{m}$ is nearly double the standard interference press-fit interval (P7: max $-0.024\text{ mm}$; min $-0.059\text{ mm}$). Consequently, a metal-cased seal (like SKF CRW1 or CRWA1) completely loses retention, spins within the housing bore, and migrates axially, causing catastrophic oil leakage.

**The HMS Advantage:** The vulcanized elastomer outer body features molded circumferential beads. The rubber retains elastic memory and continuous radial contact pressure against the aluminum bore across thermal cycles.

---

##### 4.2 Auxiliary Dust Lip (HMSA10) vs. Single Lip (HMS5)
* **Single-Lip Seals (HMS5):** Possess only the primary, spring-loaded hydrodynamic sealing lip. While effective at fluid retention, they offer zero protection against external particulate matter.
* **Dual-Lip Seals with Auxiliary Lip (HMSA10):** Integrate a secondary, non-spring-loaded elastomer lip facing the external environment.

In Formula Student racing:
1. Carbon-metallic brake pads generate microscopic abrasive dust immediately adjacent to the wheel seal.
2. Hot Hoosier racing slicks shed molten rubber debris ("marbles") and track grit.
3. If solid particles breach the sealing zone of an HMS5 seal, they embed under the lip, machining a severe circumferential wear groove into the shaft and tearing the flexible sealing edge.
4. The auxiliary lip of the HMSA10 acts as a mechanical deflector. Because it operates with minimal interference, it excludes particulates without adding parasitic friction torque or excess underlip heat.

---

##### 4.3 Fluoroelastomer (V / FKM) vs. Nitrile Rubber (RG / NBR)

| Performance Parameter | Nitrile Rubber (RG / NBR) | Fluoroelastomer (V / FKM) — Selected | Impact |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Continuous Temp Range** | $-40^\circ\text{C}$ to $+100^\circ\text{C}$ | $-20^\circ\text{C}$ to $+200^\circ\text{C}$ | Pushes contact zone temperatures to $95\text{--}105^\circ\text{C}$. |
| **Peak Temperature Spike** | Up to $+120^\circ\text{C}$ | Up to $+250^\circ\text{C}$ | Provides immunity during post-braking heat soak in the paddock when airflow ceases. |
| **Garter Spring Material** | Carbon Steel | Stainless Steel (AISI 302/304) | Eliminates spring corrosion |

---

#### 5. Operational Verification

##### 5.1 Circumferential Surface Speed
* Shaft diameter at seal: $d_1 = 85\text{ mm} = 0.085\text{ m}$
* Peak wheel rotational speed: $n = 1650\text{ rpm}$

$$v = \frac{\pi \cdot d_1 \cdot n}{60} = \frac{\pi \cdot 0.085 \cdot 1650}{60} = \mathbf{7.34\text{ m/s}}$$

* **SKF HMSA10 V Limit:** $14\text{ m/s}$ continuous / $31.2\text{ m/s}$ max catalog rating.
* **Safety Factor:** $\text{SF}_v = \frac{14}{7.34} \approx \mathbf{1.907}$

---

##### 5.2 Internal Pressure Differential

###### 5.2.2 System Boundary
With the baseline from FST15 Drivetrain Design Documentation (Section Oil Seal, pp. 33–34):
* **Total Internal Cavity Volume ($V_{\text{total}}$):** The rigid internal envelope formed by the hub, upright, and lids is $V_{\text{total}} \approx 407.4\text{ ml}$.
* **Initial Oil Charge ($V_{0,\text{oil}}$):** Liquid lubricant occupies $1/3$ of the internal volume:
  $$V_{0,\text{oil}} = \frac{1}{3} V_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{135.80\text{ ml}}$$
* **Initial Air Cushion ($V_{1,\text{air}}$):** The air occupying $2/3$ of the volume:
  $$V_{1,\text{air}} = \frac{2}{3} V_{\text{total}} = \mathbf{271.60\text{ ml}}$$
* **Thermal Boundary Conditions:**
  * Initial assembly state: $T_1 = 15^\circ\text{C} = 15 + 273.15 = \mathbf{288.15\text{ K}}$, at atmospheric pressure $p_1 = p_{\text{atm}} = \mathbf{1.00\text{ bar}}$.
  * Worst-case operating state: $T_2 = 100^\circ\text{C} = 100 + 273.15 = \mathbf{373.15\text{ K}}$.
  * Effective thermal delta: $\Delta T = T_2 - T_1 = 100 - 15 = \mathbf{85\text{ K}}$.
* **Oil Expansion Coefficient ($\beta$):** The volumetric thermal expansion coefficient for synthetic transmission gear oils is $\beta = 7.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ K}^{-1}$.

###### 5.2.3 Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

1. **Volumetric Thermal Expansion of the Liquid Oil:**
   The volume increase of the liquid lubricant under thermal excitation is given by:
   $$\Delta V_{\text{oil}} = V_{0,\text{oil}} \cdot \beta \cdot \Delta T = 135.80\text{ ml} \times (7.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ K}^{-1}) \times 85\text{ K} = \mathbf{8.08\text{ ml}}$$
   The expanded oil volume at operating temperature becomes:
   $$V_{2,\text{oil}} = V_{0,\text{oil}} + \Delta V_{\text{oil}} = 135.80\text{ ml} + 8.08\text{ ml} = \mathbf{143.88\text{ ml}}$$

2. **Compression of the Trapped Air Headspace:**
   Assuming a structurally rigid aluminum housing ($V_{\text{total}} = \text{constant}$), the expansion of the liquid oil directly reduces the available volume for the trapped air:
   $$V_{2,\text{air}} = V_{1,\text{air}} - \Delta V_{\text{oil}}$$
   $$V_{2,\text{air}} = 271.60\text{ ml} - 8.08\text{ ml} = \mathbf{263.52\text{ ml}}$$

3. **Calculation of Final Internal Air Pressure (Combined Ideal Gas Law):**
   $$p \cdot V = n \cdot R \cdot T$$
   Because the wheel hub is hermetically enclosed by the radial shaft seal and stationary O-rings:
   * **Zero Mass Transfer:** No air can escape the cavity, and no ambient air can enter ($m = \text{constant}$).
   * **Constant State Product:** The product of the trapped air mass and the gas constant ($n \cdot R$) remains strictly constant throughout all thermal transitions.

   Rearranging the state equation by dividing by $T$:
   $$\frac{p_1 \cdot V_{1,\text{air}}}{T_1} = \frac{p_2 \cdot V_{2,\text{air}}}{T_2}$$

   Solving explicitly for the final absolute internal pressure ($p_2$):
   $$p_2 = p_1 \cdot \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{V_{1,\text{air}}}{V_{2,\text{air}}}\right)$$

   Substituting the numerical parameters:
   $$p_2 = 1.00\text{ bar} \cdot \left(\frac{373.15\text{ K}}{288.15\text{ K}}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{271.60\text{ ml}}{263.52\text{ ml}}\right)$$
   $$p_2 = 1.00 \cdot (1.2950) \cdot (1.0307) = \mathbf{1.3347\text{ bar}} \approx \mathbf{1.33\text{ bar}}$$

4. **Net Differential Pressure Across the Sealing Lip ($\Delta p$):**
   The relative pressure acting outward across the SKF HMSA10 V sealing lip is:
   $$\Delta p = p_2 - p_{\text{atm}} = 1.3347\text{ bar} - 1.00\text{ bar} = \mathbf{0.3347\text{ bar}} \approx \mathbf{0.33\text{ bar}} \quad (0.033\text{ MPa})$$

   Comparing the calculated operating differential pressure against the maximum catalog rating of the SKF HMSA10 V:
   $$\Delta p = 0.33\text{ bar} < \Delta p_{\text{max}} = 0.50\text{ bar} \implies \text{The HMSA10 V can withstand the thermal pressurization.}$$

Justification:
### Front Plate Trade Study

#### 1. Summary & Context
In previous Formula Student prototypes (e.g., FST14/FST15 with AMK DD5 motors), a dedicated **Motor Front Plate** was incorporated into the wheel assembly to fulfill two critical functions:
1. **Cooling Jacket O-Ring Sealing:** Providing a machined sealing face and groove to isolate the motor cooling jacket from the transmission cavity.
2. **Mechanical Stoppage:** Providing machined positive-locking slots/keys to react the motor stator torque reaction against the upright.

For the **FST16** architecture, the powertrain transitions to the **DTI F-MOT** motor. This study demonstrates that both historical functions have been rendered completely obsolete by the motor's design.

---

#### 2. Functional Redundancy Analysis

##### 2.1 Resolution of Sealing Interface (Function 1)
The AMK motor lacked an integrated front sealing surface. The **DTI F-MOT** features an integrated front-face O-ring groove and sealing land. The motor seals directly against the upright mounting face, entirely eliminating the requirement for an intermediate plate.

##### 2.2 Resolution of Stator Torque Reaction (Function 2)
The legacy architecture relied on positive mechanical dogs/slots machined into the front plate to prevent motor casing rotation. To evaluate whether positive mechanical stops are required for the DTI motor, a fastener joint analysis was conducted under worst-case motor torque.

---

#### 3. Quantitative Structural & Fastener Failure Mode Analysis
The motor stator reacts against the upright through a circular pattern of **$6 \times \text{M}4$ bolts**.

##### 3.1 Input Parameters

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Units | Description / Source |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Peak Motor Stator Torque** | $T_{\text{motor}}$ | **$31.6$** | $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ | Maximum peak torque capacity of DTI F-MOT |
| **Bolt Circle Diameter** | $D_{\text{p}}$ | **$70.0$** | $\text{mm}$ | Bolt circle diameter ($r = 0.035\text{ m}$) |
| **Fastener Specification** | — | **$6 \times \text{M}4$** | — | Grade 12.9 (Grade 10.9 baseline) |
| **Fastener Tensile Stress Area** | $A_t$ | **$8.78$** | $\text{mm}^2$ | Standard ISO metric M4 thread area |
| **Fastener Core (Minor) Area** | $A_{\text{core}}$ | **$7.24$** | $\text{mm}^2$ | Shear plane across minor thread diameter |
| **Tightening Torque** | $T_{\text{tight}}$ | **$4.0$** | $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ | Assembly torque |
| **Torque-Preload Coefficient** | $K$ | **$0.20$** | — | Standard zinc-plated / unlubricated coefficient |
| **Friction Coefficient** | $\mu$ | **$0.15$** | — | Metal-on-metal interface (Al 7075-T6 to Steel) |
| **Upright Flange Thickness** | $t_{\text{flange}}$ | **$5.0$** | $\text{mm}$ | Minimum flange thickness of upright |
| **Upright Material** | — | **Al 7075-T6** | — | $S_y = 503\text{ MPa}$, $S_u = 572\text{ MPa}$ |

---

##### 3.2 Applied Tangential Shear Force
The total tangential reaction force required to balance peak motor torque across the bolt circle radius ($r = 35\text{ mm}$):

$$F_{\text{total, shear}} = \frac{T_{\text{motor}}}{r} = \frac{31.6\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}{0.035\text{ m}} = \mathbf{902.86\text{ N}}$$

Evenly distributed across the $n = 6$ fasteners:

$$P_{\text{bolt}} = \frac{F_{\text{total, shear}}}{6} = \frac{902.86\text{ N}}{6} = \mathbf{150.48\text{ N per bolt}}$$

---

##### 3.3 Failure Mode 1: Joint Friction Slip (Primary Load Path)
In a properly preloaded bolted assembly, tangential shear must be reacted entirely by **interface friction clamped by bolt pretension**, preventing any joint micro-slip or cyclical fastener bending.

1. **Bolt Axial Preload ($F_i$):**
   $$F_i = \frac{T_{\text{tight}}}{K \cdot d} = \frac{4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}{0.20 \times 0.004\text{ m}} = \mathbf{5000\text{ N}} \quad (5.0\text{ kN per bolt})$$

2. **Bolt Tensile Stress & Preload Safety Factor:**
   $$\sigma_{\text{axial}} = \frac{F_i}{A_t} = \frac{5000\text{ N}}{8.78\text{ mm}^2} = \mathbf{569.48\text{ MPa}}$$
   For Class 12.9 fasteners ($S_y = 1100\text{ MPa}$):
   $$n_{\text{preload}} = \frac{S_y}{\sigma_{\text{axial}}} = \frac{1100\text{ MPa}}{569.48\text{ MPa}} = \mathbf{1.93} \quad (\text{Highly Safe})$$

3. **Joint Frictional Clamping Torque Capacity ($T_{\text{friction}}$):**
   $$T_{\text{friction}} = \mu \cdot \left(\sum F_i\right) \cdot r = \mu \cdot (n \cdot F_i) \cdot r$$
   $$T_{\text{friction}} = 0.15 \cdot (6 \times 5000\text{ N}) \cdot 0.035\text{ m} = \mathbf{157.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}$$

4. **Safety Factor Against Joint Slip ($n_{\text{slip}}$):**
   $$n_{\text{slip}} = \frac{T_{\text{friction}}}{T_{\text{motor}}} = \frac{157.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}{31.6\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}} = \mathbf{4.98} \quad (\approx \mathbf{5.0})$$

**Joint Slip Conclusion:** The clamping friction capacity ($157.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) is **5 times greater** than the maximum motor torque ($31.6\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$). Under all racing conditions, the joint will remain 100% slip-free.

---

##### 3.4 Failure Mode 2: Bolt Direct Shear (Worst-Case Slipped Joint)
Assuming complete loss of friction (e.g., severe grease contamination where $\mu \to 0$):

1. **Direct Shear Stress across Minor Thread Diameter:**
   $$\tau = \frac{P_{\text{bolt}}}{A_{\text{core}}} = \frac{150.48\text{ N}}{7.24\text{ mm}^2} = \mathbf{20.78\text{ MPa}}$$

2. **Shear Yield Strength (Von Mises Distortion Energy Criterion):**
   $$S_{sy} = 0.577 \cdot S_y$$
   * For Class 12.9 ($S_y = 1100\text{ MPa}$): $S_{sy} = 0.577 \times 1100 = \mathbf{634.70\text{ MPa}}$
   * For Class 10.9 ($S_y = 940\text{ MPa}$): $S_{sy} = 0.577 \times 940 = \mathbf{542.38\text{ MPa}}$

3. **Safety Factor to Fastener Shear ($n_{\text{shear}}$):**
   $$n_{\text{shear (12.9)}} = \frac{S_{sy}}{\tau} = \frac{634.70\text{ MPa}}{20.78\text{ MPa}} = \mathbf{30.5} \quad (\text{Immense Reserve})$$
   $$n_{\text{shear (10.9)}} = \frac{542.38\text{ MPa}}{20.78\text{ MPa}} = \mathbf{26.1}$$

---

##### 3.5 Failure Mode 3: Upright Flange Hole Crushing / Bearing Stress
If the joint slips and the bolt shanks bear directly against the hole walls in the Al 7075-T6 upright:

1. **Projected Bearing Area:**
   $$A_b = t_{\text{flange}} \cdot d_{\text{bolt}} = 5.0\text{ mm} \times 4.0\text{ mm} = \mathbf{20.00\text{ mm}^2}$$

2. **Hole Wall Bearing Stress ($\sigma_{\text{bearing}}$):**
   $$\sigma_{\text{bearing}} = \frac{P_{\text{bolt}}}{A_b} = \frac{150.48\text{ N}}{20.00\text{ mm}^2} = \mathbf{7.52\text{ MPa}}$$

3. **Safety Factor Against Hole Wall Yielding ($n_{\text{bearing}}$):**
   $$n_{\text{bearing}} = \frac{S_{y, \text{Al 7075-T6}}}{\sigma_{\text{bearing}}} = \frac{503.0\text{ MPa}}{7.52\text{ MPa}} = \mathbf{66.9} \quad (\text{Zero Risk of Elongation})$$

---

#### 4. Summary Matrix Across Bolt Property Classes

| Sizing & Failure Mode (In Sequence) | Class 12.9 (Optimal) | Class 10.9 (Standard) | Class 8.8 (Commercial) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Applied Bolt Load (Slipped State)** | $150.5\text{ N}$ | $150.5\text{ N}$ | $150.5\text{ N}$ |
| **1. Bolt Core Shear Stress ($\tau$)** | $20.8\text{ MPa}$ | $20.8\text{ MPa}$ | $20.8\text{ MPa}$ |
| **Safety Factor: Bolt Shear ($n_{\text{shear}}$)** | **30.5** *(Immense)* | **26.1** *(Immense)* | **18.2** *(Highly Safe)* |
| **2. Joint Frictional Torque Capacity** | $157.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ | $157.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ | $157.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ |
| **Safety Factor: Joint Slip ($n_{\text{slip}}$)** | **4.98** *(Immense)* | **4.98** *(Immense)* | **4.98** *(Immense)* |
| **Safety Factor: Preload Yield** | **1.93** *(Safe)* | **1.68** *(Safe)* | **1.16** *(Critical Risk)* |
| **3. Upright Hole Bearing Stress** | $7.52\text{ MPa}$ | $7.52\text{ MPa}$ | $7.52\text{ MPa}$ |
| **Safety Factor: Hole Wall Crushing** | **66.9** *(Immense)* | **66.9** *(Immense)* | **66.9** *(Immense)* |

---

#### 5. Conclusion
**Decision: The Front Plate is declared completely obsolete and is permanently eliminated from the FST16 assembly.**

* **Zero Functional Need:** The DTI motor provides native O-ring sealing, and the $6 \times \text{M}4$ bolt circle provides a **$5\times$ safety factor against friction slip** ($157.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ capacity vs. $31.6\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ demand), making anti-rotation slots redundant.
* **Unsprung Mass Reduction:** Eliminates component mass and fastener overhead.
* **Manufacturing & Simplicity:** Removes an intermediate machined interface, eliminates stacked tolerances, and enables direct, rigid motor mounting to the upright structure.

Description: Baseline motor back plate iteration for FST15 carry-over.
Justification:
### Backplate Rationale

#### Component Trade-Off Study: Back Plate

##### 1. Functional Definition
The Motor Back Plate serves as an interface between the upright structure and the electric motor housing, fulfilling three primary engineering functions:

* **Elimination of Blind O-Ring Assembly:** Provides an open, visually accessible installation plane for the motor cooling jacket O-ring, eliminating the risk of seal loss.
* **Direct Inspection & Rapid Maintenance:** Enables independent visual inspection and leak checks without requiring full motor extraction.
* **Uniform Seal:** With the recommendation from DTI of using F6 for the internal upright geometry of the interface with the motor, this could lead to uneven force on the O-ring if the machined upright does come with a looser geometry.

---

##### 2. Marginal Mass Delta vs. System Risk
Integrating the back plate into the main upright body yields a possible mass reduction of approximately $\approx 20\text{ g}$ against its $40\text{ g}$ baseline. This marginal $20\text{ g}$ saving is heavily outweighed by the heightened operational and manufacturing risks.

---

##### 3. Risk Mitigation
The FST16 powertrain introduces significant major subsystem redesigns, including:
* Transition to the DTI F-MOT motor architecture;
* Integration of the new planetary gearset;
* Complete redesign of drivetrain.

Carrying over a proven, back plate design preserves known interface geometry, avoids development variables, and eliminates unnecessary design risk.

---

##### 4. Conclusion
**Decision: The decoupled Back Plate component is retained for the FST16 wheel assembly.**

The marginal mass saving ($\approx 20\text{ g}$) of one piece integration is unjustified when evaluated against the benefits in sealing reliability, manufacturing simplicity, trackside serviceability, reducing overall risk.
